title: Identify and treat shared mechanisms of neurodegeneration across diseases

concept.text: The proposed innovation is to identify a biological process that causally contributes to degeneration in distinct neurological diseases, then show that treating that process produces meaningful clinical benefit across those diseases. Diseases with different initiating proteins or genetic causes might converge on a shared downstream vulnerability. Establishing that convergence would require distinguishing a mechanism that contributes to damage from a response that merely accompanies it.

The integrated stress response, or ISR, illustrates this approach. The supplied review describes associations between persistent ISR activation or dysfunction and both amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Alzheimer disease. Such associations motivate therapeutic experiments, but they do not establish that ISR dysfunction drives either disease or that suppressing it will help patients. Shared biomarker changes, rescue in disease models, and clinical benefit in humans are separate evidentiary steps.

Conceptual scope: success would not require discovering one universal “master regulator.” A mechanism that can be treated effectively in several biologically distinct diseases would satisfy the central ambition even if other diseases require different interventions. Preserving surviving neurons, arresting further deterioration, and restoring lost function are also distinct capabilities; achieving one would not establish the others.

significance.text: Conditional significance: demonstrating a treatable shared causal mechanism could give a therapy broader clinical reach than an intervention developed around one diagnosis alone. It could also allow mechanistic insights from one disease to inform treatment development in another. This would be revolutionary because it would establish a reusable therapeutic principle across distinct diseases, rather than only a recurring biological association.

The ISR provides a concrete scientific rationale for pursuing that possibility. The reviewed article reports neuroprotection and functional benefits from ISR inhibition in models of ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases. Those findings support further investigation, but the underlying model studies were not separately supplied or inspected in the review, and their reported benefits do not establish efficacy across human diagnoses.

Conditional downstream possibilities include grouping patients by a demonstrated disease mechanism, sharing some drug-development knowledge across diagnoses, and combining protection from further degeneration with separate repair treatments. These possibilities depend on the mechanism being active, harmful, and therapeutically accessible in the relevant patients. A common pathway does not guarantee a common effective dose, treatment window, or magnitude of benefit.

An important limit on the impact is that stopping degeneration would not by itself replace neurons already lost, reconnect disrupted circuits, or restore learned function. A broadly protective treatment could therefore be transformative while still leaving substantial disability. Claims of reversal would require additional evidence of functional recovery and the biological repair responsible for it.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a reproducible chain of evidence connecting a shared mechanism to disease causation and then to durable clinical benefit in distinct human neurodegenerative diseases. The ISR example shows the gap: cross-disease associations and reported model benefits supplied a therapeutic rationale, but the tested DNL343 regimen did not demonstrate slower ALS progression.

Scientific synthesis: mechanistic studies must determine whether a shared pathway contributes to damage, reflects an attempted protective response, or has different effects at different disease stages. They must also establish which cells and patient subgroups depend on that pathway. Observing the same biomarker in two diseases cannot resolve these questions, and a causal contribution in one disease cannot simply be assumed in another.

A concrete engineering and measurement barrier is confirming that an intervention produces the intended biological effect in the relevant human tissue during treatment. The reviewed DNL343 trial had incomplete confirmation of target engagement, limiting what its negative clinical result can establish about the ISR mechanism. Without sufficient evidence of biological activity, failure to improve outcomes cannot decisively distinguish an ineffective treatment regimen from an unsuitable therapeutic target.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: translation also requires adequate drug exposure, tolerable sustained pathway modulation, appropriate treatment timing, and outcome measures that capture meaningful changes in each disease. If recovery is part of the intended capability, an additional breakthrough must explain how damaged tissue or circuits regain function. Neuroprotection alone does not supply that repair mechanism.

current_state.text: The supplied evidence establishes a candidate shared-pathway rationale and a completed clinical test of one intervention, rather than achievement of the proposed cross-disease capability. The reviewed article describes ISR abnormalities associated with ALS and Alzheimer disease and reports earlier model evidence of neuroprotection and functional benefit. It also describes prior biomarker modulation. These findings occupy different evidentiary levels and do not collectively demonstrate clinical benefit across diseases.

Paganoni and colleagues’ randomized clinical trial, published on September 22, 2026, tested DNL343 in people with ALS. DNL343 is a brain-penetrant small molecule designed to inhibit the ISR by activating eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B, or eIF2B. At 200 mg daily during 24 weeks of placebo-controlled treatment, it showed no evidence of slowing disease progression. The reported disease rate ratio was 1.04, with a 95% credible interval of 0.83–1.32; the article reported no significant differences in primary or secondary outcomes.

This result limits efficacy claims for that dose and treatment duration in the studied ALS population. The estimate and its uncertainty do not prove an effect of exactly zero, and they do not establish failure under every possible treatment condition. Incomplete confirmation of target engagement further limits mechanistic interpretation. The result therefore does not, on its own, justify abandoning ISR targeting or rejecting all hypotheses about shared mechanisms of neurodegeneration.

The supplied review assessed a retained full-article XML containing methods, results, discussion, and references, with no reported truncation or extraction problems. Linked supplements and the underlying studies cited for model benefits were not separately supplied or inspected. The bounded freshness-search record was empty, so the materials do not establish whether subsequent evidence changed the broader field after the September 2026 report, including by the review’s November 1, 2026 checkpoint. That coverage limitation does not undermine the dated trial result.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent mechanistic studies should establish a target’s causal contribution in at least two biologically distinct human neurodegenerative diseases, followed by controlled trials showing durable, clinically meaningful benefit in each. Two diseases is a proposed minimum for demonstrating cross-disease reach, not an established consensus threshold. Even convincing results would establish breadth in the tested diseases and populations, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Causal target produces durable, meaningful clinical benefit in two distinct diseases

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidentiary requirements: studies should connect intervention exposure to target engagement and relevant downstream effects, then connect those effects to patient outcomes. Biomarker changes or model rescue should support the causal account without substituting for clinical benefit. Independent replication should test whether the result survives changes in investigators, sites, and relevant patient characteristics.
completion_criteria.label: Independently replicated evidence links intervention exposure through target engagement to outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: trials should define disease distinctness, eligible populations, disease stage, dose, treatment duration, meaningful benefit, and durability before interpreting results. Follow-up should establish whether benefits persist and whether sustained treatment remains tolerable. Conclusions should identify where benefit has been demonstrated and where extrapolation remains uncertain; a shared target need not yield an identical regimen or response across diagnoses.
completion_criteria.label: Trials predefine treatment boundaries and report durability, tolerability, and extrapolation limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reversal criterion: a claim of reversal should additionally demonstrate recovery of previously lost function and provide evidence for the repair mechanism responsible. Slower decline, stabilization, and improved biomarkers should be reported as their respective outcomes. Functional improvement alone would also need interpretation sufficient to distinguish repair from compensation or symptomatic benefit.
completion_criteria.label: Reversal demonstrates lost function recovery through an evidenced repair mechanism

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NRL-09, “Prevent Alzheimer’s dementia before irreversible functional loss,” and NRL-11, “Halt established Alzheimer’s disease and restore lost function,” could benefit from a validated shared mechanism. Their goals remain specific to Alzheimer disease and particular intervention stages. NRL-15 requires benefit across distinct diseases; NRL-11 additionally requires restoration, which a protective shared-pathway treatment would not automatically deliver.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” addresses a complementary repair capability. NRL-05, spinal-cord regeneration with functional reconnection, and NRL-16, biological repair of the injured visual pathway, likewise focus on rebuilding function after injury. A shared neuroprotective mechanism might help preserve tissue relevant to these efforts, but protection would not establish replacement, reconnection, or preservation of learned information.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-10, “Safe, programmable delivery to selected cells throughout the human brain,” could enable some shared-mechanism therapies by making relevant cells accessible. Delivery is nevertheless a separate capability: successful delivery does not establish that the target causes disease or that modifying it benefits patients, and a broadly useful neurodegeneration treatment need not require the full delivery capability envisioned by NRL-10.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-18, determining and interrupting the disease process associated with chronic traumatic encephalopathy, could investigate mechanisms that overlap with other degenerative disorders, but such overlap remains to be demonstrated. NRL-12, durable immune control and functional remyelination in multiple sclerosis, and NRL-13, protection during acute ischemic stroke, have distinct disease processes and treatment goals. Shared cellular stress responses would not by themselves establish a common effective treatment across these entries.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-02, a predictive theory of neural circuit computation, and NRL-03, whole-brain cellular-resolution recording during natural behavior, could provide ways to characterize functional disruption or recovery. They do not substitute for causal disease evidence or clinical trials. NRL-04, selective repair of specific memory traces, adds a specificity requirement beyond broadly protecting neurons, while NRL-01’s theory of consciousness is not a prerequisite for establishing a treatable shared degenerative mechanism.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-07’s communication channel for profound paralysis, NRL-08’s visual-cortex prosthesis, and NRL-17’s bidirectional movement-and-sensation interface pursue useful function through neural interfaces. Their success would not demonstrate interruption of neurodegeneration. NRL-14’s durable, non-destructive seizure freedom similarly has a distinct endpoint: an overlapping biological pathway would require separate evidence before it could connect seizure control to the cross-disease capability proposed here.

change_log.change: Preserved NRL-15’s identity and expanded the explanation of shared causal mechanisms without requiring a universal master regulator.
change_log.reason: The research and review support a coherent cross-disease therapeutic goal; a single master regulator is speculative and unnecessary to that goal.

change_log.change: Specified the DNL343 trial’s publication date, 200 mg daily dose, 24-week placebo-controlled duration, studied ALS scope, disease rate ratio, and credible interval.
change_log.reason: These details constrain interpretation of the negative efficacy result and preserve supported quantitative evidence.

change_log.change: Integrated incomplete target-engagement confirmation and distinguished absence of demonstrated benefit from proof of zero effect or rejection of the ISR pathway.
change_log.reason: The review identifies these as essential limits on the trial’s mechanistic implications.

change_log.change: Separated shared associations, biomarker modulation, reported model benefits, causal evidence, and human clinical efficacy.
change_log.reason: These are distinct evidentiary steps; combining them would overstate progress toward the innovation.

change_log.change: Developed proposed completion criteria for causality, replication, clinical durability, practical boundaries, and reversal.
change_log.reason: The review endorses these distinctions while emphasizing that the two-disease minimum and other thresholds are proposals rather than established standards.

change_log.change: Preserved full-article availability, uninspected supplements and underlying studies, and the empty freshness-search record.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports the dated trial finding but cannot establish comprehensive coverage of later evidence.

change_log.change: Explained relationships across the supplied roster while retaining each entry’s distinct endpoint.
change_log.reason: Shared mechanisms, delivery, repair, measurement, and functional interfaces may complement one another without constituting the same innovation.

unresolved_issues: The supplied materials do not establish whether later evidence changed the field after the September 22, 2026 DNL343 report.
Incomplete target-engagement confirmation leaves unresolved how decisively the tested regimen evaluated the intended ISR mechanism.
The materials do not establish a shared target with independently demonstrated causal importance and durable clinical benefit across distinct human neurodegenerative diseases.
The underlying model studies and linked trial supplements were not separately inspected in the supplied review, limiting independent assessment of those details.
Disease distinctness, clinically meaningful benefit, durability, and recovery endpoints still require operational definitions for a concrete demonstration program.
Whether any successful shared-pathway treatment could also support neuronal repair and functional restoration remains unresolved.

brief.title: Treating shared causes of nerve cell loss
possible: People with different diseases that destroy nerve cells could receive treatments aimed at a shared cause of damage. A treatment developed for one diagnosis could also help people with another, even when their diseases begin differently.
why: A shared treatment could reach more patients, and discoveries in one disease could guide treatment in another. Patients could be grouped by the harmful biological process they share, giving drug development a route across diagnostic boundaries.

sources.who: Sabrina Paganoni and the HEALEY ALS Platform Trial Study Group
sources.showed: People with ALS, a disease that destroys movement-controlling nerve cells, received DNL343 or an inactive treatment. The drug showed no evidence of slowing decline over 24 weeks.
sources.cited_for: This trial tests whether dampening cells' stress response can slow disease in patients.
sources.not_established: The result does not establish benefit across diseases or settle whether the intended biological process was sufficiently altered.

sources.showed: DNL343 reduced signs of the integrated stress response, cells' reaction to stress, in blood cells and fluid around the brain and spinal cord in ALS participants. In mice, it briefly delayed movement problems and nerve cell damage.
sources.quote: ISR activation was observed in ALS patient spinal cord and CSF.
sources.cited_for: The work connects effects in disease models with measurable biological changes in people.
sources.not_established: Changes in biological markers and temporary benefits in mice do not establish lasting clinical benefit across human diseases.

shown: Researchers have reached human trials with a drug aimed at a candidate shared process. Early studies found biological changes, but Paganoni and colleagues' later ALS trial found no evidence of slower decline. Nobody has established a shared causal process whose treatment delivers lasting clinical benefit across distinct diseases.
missing: Independent studies still need to establish that a shared process causes damage in distinct diseases, rather than merely accompanying it.
Treatment must produce the intended biological effect in the relevant human tissue and connect that effect to patient benefit.
Controlled trials still need to demonstrate lasting, meaningful benefit across diseases.

milestones.label: A shared cause yields lasting benefit across diseases
milestones.explanation: Independent studies and controlled trials would have to connect a shared cause of damage to lasting, meaningful benefit in two distinct human diseases. This would establish treatment reach across diagnoses.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce the treatment's chain of effects
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the chain from drug exposure through its intended biological action to patient outcomes. This would connect clinical benefit to the proposed cause of damage.

milestones.label: Trials establish who benefits and under what conditions
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to predefine diseases, patients, disease stage, dosing, duration and meaningful benefit, then report lasting effects and tolerability. This would establish treatment boundaries and limits on extending the findings.

milestones.label: Recovered function is linked to biological repair
milestones.explanation: A reversal claim would have to demonstrate recovery of lost function and evidence of the repair responsible. This would distinguish repair from slower decline, compensation or temporary symptom relief.

uncertain: Did the tested DNL343 treatment sufficiently alter the stress response in the relevant tissue to judge whether that process is a useful target?
How should disease distinctness, meaningful benefit and lasting effects be defined when judging success?
Could a treatment that protects surviving nerve cells also support repair and recovery of lost function?

page.title: Disease-modifying therapy for shared neurodegenerative mechanisms
page.definition: Treatments acting on the same biological process slow clinical decline in at least two distinct diseases that progressively destroy nerve cells. Experiments show that changing the process affects a disease-relevant function, such as neuron survival. Studies in people with each diagnosis show both that treatment changes the process and that patients decline more slowly.

goal.need: In 2021 an estimated 6.25 million Americans were living with Alzheimer dementia, which progressively erodes the ability to manage daily tasks. ALS takes away voluntary movement and has a median survival of 20–48 months. Riluzole prolonged survival in ALS trials without a measurable benefit in muscle strength. Where the same process injures neurons in different diseases, slowing that injury could give people more time to manage daily tasks or move independently. The benefit depends on how much the process contributes to decline in each disease.

statements.body: National Institute on Aging, FY 2020 Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Bypass Budget Milestones, milestone 2.H
statements.quote: Launch a minimum of three drug discovery projects targeting pathways common across AD and at least two other neurodegenerative disorders.
statements.context: The programme also calls for preclinical validation of at least three new therapeutic targets shared by Alzheimer disease and at least two other neurodegenerative disorders. Both counts apply to the research programme.

completion.title: Shared-mechanism treatments receive traditional approvals to slow two neurodegenerative diseases.
completion.criterion: For at least two distinct neurodegenerative diagnoses, therapies acting on the same experimentally validated mechanism receive FDA traditional approval for slowing clinical progression. Human studies demonstrate modulation of that mechanism in each diagnosis. Symptom relief or accelerated approval based only on an unverified surrogate does not satisfy this test. Populations, treatment effects and follow-up are those accepted for each indication.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; synthesis of NIH's shared-mechanism goal and FDA's disease-specific traditional approval criterion.
completion.basis: Searches of NIH/NIA programmes, FDA development criteria, ICH E9 and cross-disease trials found no cross-diagnosis completion rule. The Atlas combines disease-specific traditional approvals with shared-mechanism evidence; two is its minimum for more than one diagnosis. FDA states: “Traditional approval requires that clinical benefit be shown before approval can be granted.”

milestones.title: Changing a candidate shared target corrects a disease-relevant function in an experimental model.
milestones.criterion: In a cell or animal model of the diagnosis, changing the expression or activity of the candidate target normalizes a functional measurement selected to represent the disease state.
milestones.set_by: NINDS, RFA-NS-19-015, phenotypic target-validation criterion for Alzheimer’s disease-related dementias. Its use in other diagnoses is by analogy.
milestones.threshold_quote: modulation leads to the normalization or impairment of the functional read outs selected to represent respectively the disease or control states

milestones.title: A candidate shared-mechanism treatment is administered to people under an effective IND.
milestones.criterion: An investigator administers the candidate treatment to a participant under an effective US investigational new drug application (IND). The IND takes effect 30 days after FDA receives it unless FDA places the investigation on clinical hold, or earlier if FDA notifies the sponsor that the investigation may begin.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.40, requirements for investigational human administration in the United States.
milestones.threshold_quote: An investigator may not administer an investigational new drug to human subjects until the IND goes into effect

milestones.title: A candidate treatment meets early human safety criteria and demonstrates pathway activity.
milestones.criterion: Early human studies meet their programme's safety/tolerability decision criteria and show biological activity through target engagement or a downstream pharmacodynamic response. No universal numerical cutoff is specified. In DNL343's ALS study, the 200 mg/day group had about 80% median reduction in ATF4 protein and CHAC1 gene-expression responses in stimulated blood cells at day 28 (6 participants per assay). These are integrated stress response markers: indicators of the cellular response to stress. This establishes peripheral pathway modulation, without establishing engagement in human brain tissue.
milestones.set_by: NIA, PAR-25-226 early clinical development criteria; written for non-amyloid/non-tau treatments for Alzheimer disease and related dementias.
milestones.threshold_quote: Evaluation of whether an intervention produces sufficient evidence of short-term activity

milestones.title: A candidate shared-mechanism treatment meets its protocol's clinical efficacy threshold.
milestones.criterion: Treatment meets the protocol’s primary clinical efficacy rule for the diagnosis. In HEALEY ALS regimen G, the posterior probability that the treatment-to-placebo disease-rate ratio is below 1 must exceed 0.975, with function and survival modeled jointly over 24 weeks. In the amended Alzheimer disease protocol AB09004, treatment must outperform placebo on change from baseline to week 24 in cognition (ADAS-cog) or activities of daily living (ADCS-ADL), at a significance level of 0.025.
milestones.set_by: HEALEY ALS Platform Trial investigators, regimen G primary analysis, for ALS; AB Science, study AB09004 amended primary analysis, for Alzheimer disease. Each numerical threshold applies only to its named protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: the posterior probability that the DRR less than 1 is greater than 0.975.

milestones.title: Confirmatory trials establish clinical benefit and an acceptable benefit–risk relationship.
milestones.criterion: Confirmatory controlled trials establish the claimed clinical benefit and estimate its size with enough precision to judge its clinical significance. The evidence supports the claim in a defined patient population, and the development programme establishes a dose and schedule with an acceptable balance of benefit and risk.
milestones.set_by: International Conference on Harmonisation, ICH E9, sections 2.1.1 and 2.1.2, on clinical development and confirmatory trials.
milestones.threshold_quote: Firm evidence in support of claims requires that the results of the confirmatory trials demonstrate that the investigational product under test has clinical benefits.

milestones.title: Independent laboratories reproduce the functional effect of changing the target using different methods.
milestones.criterion: After demonstrating technical feasibility, collaborating independent laboratories measure the functional consequences of changing the candidate target and cross-validate the effect using different experimental methods.
milestones.set_by: NINDS, RFA-NS-19-015, UH3 validation phase for Alzheimer’s disease-related dementias. Its use in other diagnoses is by analogy.
milestones.threshold_quote: cross-validate the impact of the target modulation in different modalities across collaborating laboratories

milestones.title: A candidate meets its prespecified phase 1 safety and tolerability criteria for further testing.
milestones.criterion: Phase 1 observations meet the programme’s prespecified safety and tolerability criteria for advancing the candidate to later clinical studies.
milestones.set_by: NIA, PAR-25-226, phase 1 transition criteria for non-amyloid, non-tau interventions in Alzheimer disease and related dementias. Their use in other diagnoses is by analogy.
milestones.threshold_quote: prespecified, go/no-go safety and tolerability milestones that must be met to advance from phase 1

milestones.title: A human study shows that treatment acts on the candidate shared pathway.
milestones.criterion: A human study shows short-term activity on the proposed pathway through target engagement or a downstream biological response to treatment. The measurement identifies the tissue or fluid in which the response was observed.
milestones.set_by: NIA, PAR-25-226, early human proof of activity for non-amyloid, non-tau interventions in Alzheimer disease and related dementias. Its use in other diagnoses is by analogy.
milestones.threshold_quote: target engagement, dose-response trends, pharmacodynamic response

not_found: No published cross-diagnosis clinical completion rule was located in the NIH/NIA programmes, FDA criteria, ICH guidance or trial documents searched.
No disease-independent numerical requirement for clinical effect size, treatment duration or target engagement was located.
No regulator, professional society or research roadmap was found that judged shared-mechanism therapy across neurodegenerative diseases unachievable or unworthy of pursuit.

references.title: Dose-ranging study of riluzole in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis/Riluzole Study Group II
references.authors: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis/Riluzole Study Group II, Lacomblez L, Bensimon G, Meininger V, Leigh PN, Guillet P

results.finding: DN9058 delayed median hindlimb clasping to 2.3 weeks in 18 treated versus 13 vehicle-treated mice.
results.detail: The effect was mild and transient; all affected mice showed clasping before week 4. The report does not establish cross-laboratory validation.
results.quote:
The time that rNLS8 mice with DN9058
dosing took to show clasping (median = 2.3 WOD) was signi ﬁcantly
longer than the rNLS8-vehicle group (median = 2 WOD) (Fig. 4f).

results.finding: DNL343 was administered in a phase 1b study randomizing 29 people with ALS.
results.detail: The paper describes DNL343 as being evaluated in clinical trials under an approved IND.
results.quote:
The participants were randomized to a 28 day
regimen of DNL343 100 mg QD (n = 10), or DNL343 200 mg QD (n =9 )
or matching placebo (n = 10), followed by an optional 18 month Open
Label Extension (OLE).

results.finding: DNL343 reduced two peripheral ISR biomarkers by a median of approximately 80% in 6 participants per assay.
results.detail: The 200 mg group showed the response at day 28; the study reported generally good tolerability. The assays establish peripheral pathway modulation, not target engagement in brain tissue.
results.quote:
ATF4 protein levels andCHAC1 gene expression
were reduced in ex vivo stimulated PBMCs throughout the dosing period
in both DNL343 dose groups, with the 200 mg dose group demon-
strating∼80% median reduction of both biomarkers at trough

results.finding: In 33 treated participants with Alzheimer disease, CSF oxidative stress marker 8‐OHdG increased 10.59% at week 24.
results.detail: The paper reports acceptable safety and tolerability and an exploratory downstream biomarker response. The oxidative stress marker is nonspecific; the result does not establish direct target engagement or whether the increase is beneficial.

results.finding: Among 393 patients in the safety dataset, serious adverse events occurred in 31% receiving high-dose masitinib.
results.detail: The trial reports safety outcomes, but it does not establish the programme's early safety decision criteria or demonstrate pathway activity.
results.quote:
Overall rates of serious AE were
31% with M4.5, 23% with M3.0, and 18% with
placebo.

results.finding: In 37 participants with Alzheimer disease, nilotinib was well tolerated and altered AD biomarkers; CSF Cmax was 4.7 nM at 300 mg.
results.quote: Nilotinib was well‐tolerated, although more adverse events, particularly mood swings, were noted with the 300 mg dose. In the nilotinib group, central nervous system (CNS) amyloid burden was significantly reduced in the frontal lobe compared to the placebo group.

results.finding: In HEALEY regimen G (n=249), 186 participants with ALS initiated DNL343.
results.quote: All randomized participants initiated treatment.

results.finding: In the DNL343 ALS trial (CSF subset n=60), week-24 CSF GDF-15 change showed no difference versus placebo.
results.detail: CSF sampling was optional, and GDF-15 changes were highly variable.
results.quote: There was no difference in GDF-15 levels in participants treated with DNL343 compared with placebo, although there was substantial variability in this outcome measure ( Figure 3 D).

results.finding: In HEALEY regimen G (n=325), DNL343 had a posterior probability of 0.37 that the disease-rate ratio was below 1.
results.quote: The estimated median DRR common to ALSFRS-R and survival, in the ECC population, was 1.04 (95% credible interval [CrI], 0.83-1.32), indicating the primary end point of slowing of disease progression for DNL343 vs placebo was not met (probability of DRR <1 = 0.37).

results.finding: DN9058 delayed median hindlimb clasping by 0.3 weeks in rNLS8 mice that developed clasping (n=31).
results.detail: All rNLS8 mice developed clasping before week 4 off doxycycline and eventually failed the locomotor tests.
results.quote:
The time that rNLS8 mice with DN9058
dosing took to show clasping (median = 2.3 WOD) was signi ﬁcantly
longer than the rNLS8-vehicle group (median = 2 WOD) (Fig. 4f).

results.finding: DN9058 transiently improved motor performance across two assays in one rNLS8 cohort. The excerpt gives n=31 for clasping only.
results.detail: The study also used different cell models and assays to measure stress-granule and ISR responses.
results.quote:
In a chronic dosing study, DN9058 was able to tran-
siently slow progression of motor phenotypes in rNLS8 mice in two
independent behavioral paradigms, the rotarod and the inverted grid
suspension test.

results.finding: In the 29-participant ALS phase 1b study, 19 participants were assigned to daily oral DNL343.
results.detail: The excerpt gives neither an IND effective date nor a trial-specific statement that dosing occurred under an effective US IND.
results.quote:
The participants were randomized to a 28 day
regimen of DNL343 100 mg QD (n = 10), or DNL343 200 mg QD (n =9 )
or matching placebo (n = 10), followed by an optional 18 month Open
Label Extension (OLE).

results.finding: In the DNL343 ALS phase 1b study (n=29 randomized), there were zero serious adverse events.
results.quote:
In the Phase 1b study, DNL343 was generally well tolerated in
participants with ALS at doses of 100 or 200 mg administered daily for
28 days (Supplementary Data 2). There were no deaths, serious or
severe AEs.

results.finding: DNL343 reduced median CSF GDF-15 by 11.2% at day 28 in the 100 mg ALS arm (n=8 evaluable).
results.quote:
Finally, 28 days of DNL343
administration to ALS participants appeared to reduce CSF GDF-15 by
~10% from baseline in both dose groups (median 11.2% and 9.8% in the
100 mg and 200 mg arms, respectively), whereas a similar reduction was
not observed in the placebo group in the phase 1b study (Fig.7f).

results.finding: DNL343 missed the HEALEY ALS primary clinical endpoints at 6 months. The paper gives no sample size for this comparison.
results.detail: The peer-reviewed paper relays a topline result in its discussion without presenting the HEALEY trial analysis.
results.quote:
recent topline clinical data indicated that primary
clinical endpoints were not met after 6 months

results.finding: ISRIB at 0.2 μM restored CA1 long-term potentiation in APPswe/PS1ΔE9 mice (13–26 hippocampal slices from 6–9 mice per group).
results.detail: In the transgenic model, systemic ISRIB improved contextual memory and water-maze learning. Water-maze probe-trial retention remained impaired.
results.quote: Whereas slices from APPswe/PS1ΔE9 mice failed to maintain LTP at CA1 Schäffer collateral synapses following tetanic stimulation, treatment with ISRIB restored LTP

results.finding: At 0.2 μM, ISRIB preserved protein synthesis in amyloid-β oligomer-exposed hippocampal slices (15 mice per condition) and primary cultures (n = 3).
results.detail: The BONCAT experiments used independent cultures and independent amyloid-β oligomer preparations. The paper does not attribute the two assays to separate laboratories.

results.finding: In 3xTg-AD mice (9 ISRIB, 8 vehicle), spatial memory improved after 2 weeks of ISRIB.
results.detail: The water-maze experiment included wild-type groups. The prose reports significant improvement versus vehicle-treated 3xTg-AD mice and gives no treated-versus-wild-type result establishing normalization.
results.quote: Importantly, ISRIB treatment improved cognitive function and brain glucose metabolism in 3xTg-AD mice.

results.finding: ISRIB restored protein synthesis in inducible VAPB P56S ALS8 motor neurons (3 biological replicates, p = 0.0125).
results.detail: The reported p-value compares mutant cells with and without ISRIB. The paper describes treated mutant and treated wild-type levels as comparable.
results.quote: Protein synthesis levels in ISRIB-treated VAPB WT and VAPB P56S were comparable, indicating that ISRIB treatment restored decreased protein synthesis caused by VAPB P56S-induced ISR

results.finding: ISRIB rescued mitochondrial membrane potential in patient-derived VAPB P56S ALS8 motor neurons (3 biological replicates, p = 0.006).
results.detail: The biological replicates were separate motor-neuron differentiations from the patient-derived model.
results.quote: The motor neurons were then treated with ISRIB and showed that treatment with ISRIB reverses this decrease in the MMP, rescuing the phenotype

results.finding: PEGASUS (N=95) included 51 participants who received sodium phenylbutyrate and taurursodiol.
results.quote: A total of 95 participants were enrolled, comprising the ITT cohort, of whom 51 were randomized to PB and TURSO and 44 were randomized to placebo

results.finding: In PEGASUS (n=67 with paired CSF), sodium phenylbutyrate and taurursodiol increased CSF 8‐OHdG by 10.59% from baseline.
results.detail: The biomarker analysis was prespecified as exploratory, with no adjustment for multiple comparisons.
results.quote:
In addition, the oxidative stress marker 8‐OHdG increased from baseline to Week 24 in the PB and TURSO group (
p
= 0.007).

results.finding: Sodium phenylbutyrate and taurursodiol missed the PEGASUS primary efficacy endpoint (N=95, p=0.36).
results.quote: Clinical efficacy outcomes did not significantly differ between treatment groups in the ITT cohort.

results.finding: Fixed-dose masitinib outperformed placebo on week-24 ADAS-cog in Alzheimer disease (n=358, p<0.001).
results.detail: The either-endpoint rule was adopted after 81% of randomized participants could have reached week 24.
results.quote: Masitinib (4.5 mg/kg/day) showed significant benefit relative to placebo over 24 weeks on the endpoint of ADAS-cog, with a δADAS-cog of −1.46 (representing an overall improvement in cognition) versus +0.69 (representing increased cognitive deterioration), respectively

results.finding: In Alzheimer disease, fixed-dose masitinib showed a 2.15-point ADAS-cog advantage over placebo (n=358).
results.detail: The 97.5% CI for masitinib minus placebo was −3.48 to −0.81 points. The activities-of-daily-living endpoint missed the protocol threshold, and the titrated regimen missed both primary endpoints.
results.quote: After 24 weeks of treatment, masitinib (4.5 mg/kg/day) significantly slowed cognitive deterioration (as measured by the primary endpoint of ADAS-cog), with acceptable safety.

results.finding: Masitinib plus riluzole met AB10015’s primary ALS efficacy rule in 201 assessable Normal Progressors (p = 0.016).
results.detail: The protocol defined the primary population in a blinded amendment after enrollment began. The broader high-dose population and both low-dose populations did not reach significance on ALSFRS-R.
results.quote:
This represents a clin-
ically meaningful 27% slowing of ALSFRS-R
deterioration over the 48-week treatment period.

results.finding: In 201 assessable ALS Normal Progressors, masitinib plus riluzole reduced ALSFRS-R decline by 3.39 points versus placebo plus riluzole.
results.detail: The confidence interval spans a 0.65- to 6.13-point benefit. Serious adverse events were more frequent at the effective dose, and the proposed dose-escalation schedule remained untested in this trial.
results.quote:
For the primary efficacy population, DALSFRS-R
showed a significant benefit for masitinib over pla-
cebo with a between-group difference in
DALSFRS-R of 3.39

results.finding: Edaravone met Study 19’s week-24 ALSFRS-R primary efficacy endpoint in 137 participants with ALS (p=0.0013).
results.detail: The review’s summary gives a conflicting enrollment count of 206. The detailed Study 19 section reports 137, consistent with its arm counts of 69 and 68.
results.quote:
The result of the applicant’s analysis of the primary endpoint was highly statistically significant (LS 
Mean change from Baseline in ALSFRS-R scores of -7.50±0.66 for placebo versus -5.01±0.64 for 
edaravone; p=0.0013).

results.finding: Edaravone reduced week-24 ALSFRS-R decline by about 2.5 points versus placebo in Study 19 (137 participants with ALS).
results.detail: The FDA review judged Study 19, the Study 16 subgroup findings, and the open-label extension together to provide substantial evidence of effectiveness. Controlled evidence of durability beyond 24 weeks was unavailable, and postmarketing reports suggested a hypersensitivity risk.
results.quote:
In 
addition, the roughly 2.5-point treatment difference favoring edaravone over only a 24-week 
period is clinically meaningful.

results.finding: Across two placebo-controlled ALS trials, 313 participants received riluzole 50 mg twice daily.
results.quote:
In the placebo-controlled clinical trials in patients with ALS (Study 1 and 2), a total of 313 
patients received RILUTEK 50 mg twice daily [see Clinical Studies (14)].

results.finding: Riluzole in ALS Study 2 (959 enrolled) had a prespecified log-rank p=0.076 for time to tracheostomy or death.
results.detail: The recommended-dose comparison in Study 2 included 236 riluzole and 242 placebo participants. The full enrollment also included other dose groups.
results.quote:
Although these survival curves were 
not statistically significantly different when evaluated by the analysis specified in the study 
protocol (Logrank test p=0.076), the difference was found to be significant by another 
appropriate analysis (Wilcoxon test p=0.05).

results.finding: Riluzole ALS trials enrolled 1,114 patients. In Study 2, median survival differed by about 60 days among those who reached tracheostomy or death.
results.detail: Muscle strength and neurological function showed no benefit. The label identifies hepatic injury as a serious risk and directs aminotransferase monitoring.
results.quote:
Among the patients in whom the endpoint of tracheostomy or death was reached during the 
study, the difference in median survival between RILUTEK and placebo was approximately 60 
days.

results.finding: In 394 adults with ALS, masitinib plus riluzole showed no difference from placebo plus riluzole in 48-week ALSFRS-R change.
results.detail: The source gives no numerical effect estimate or protocol decision threshold for the masitinib study.
results.quote: the study found no difference between the medicine and placebo in the main measure of effectiveness for the total study population and had several methodological issues.

results.finding: EMA judged masitinib’s benefit–risk balance unfavorable for ALS after reviewing a 48-week controlled study of 394 adults.
results.detail: Good clinical practice inspections identified unresolved study-conduct issues. EMA also cited methodological problems and no difference on the primary outcome in the full study population.
results.quote: Therefore, the Agency maintained its opinion that the benefits of Masitinib AB Science did not outweigh its risks and recommended refusing marketing authorisation.

results.finding: AMX0035 at 200 µM per component reduced Aβ42 in pre-plaque Tg2576 mice (sample size unreported).
results.detail: The sponsor also reports >90% neuronal viability in a separate peroxide-injury assay. The text does not establish that this assay modeled Alzheimer disease.
results.quote:
AMX0035 treatment 
significantly reduced soluble amyloid beta, preferentially Aβ42 (Figure 1).

results.finding: In amyloid-β-injected rats treated with ISRIB (n=8), hippocampal synaptic responses recovered to 90.1% of baseline after conditioning.
results.detail: The treated group differed from amyloid-β plus vehicle (P=0.0011). The comparison with reverse-peptide controls detected no difference (P=0.7370).
results.quote: Systemic administration of the small-molecule inhibitor of the ISR called ISRIB (trans-isomer) prevents Aβ-facilitated LTD and abrogates spatial learning and memory deficits in the hippocampus in exogenous synthetic Aβ-injected rats.

results.finding: ISRIB improved survival of G93A SOD1 rat cortical neurons at 500 nM in pooled experiments (n = 3 and 5 experiments across the two survival panels).
results.detail: The direct PERK inhibitor GSK2606414 failed to improve survival. The 5XUPRE reporter normalization was measured in three experiments tracking about 100 neurons per condition per experiment.
results.quote: Importantly, ISRIB enhanced the survival of G93A SOD1-expressing neurons within a wide dose range between 100nM and 10 μM (Fig.

results.finding: Mast cell depletion restored contextual freezing to wild-type-like levels in female 5XFAD mice (n in Fig. 2C, genotype interaction p = 0.043).
results.detail: Baseline freezing, cued freezing, and anxiety-like behavior showed no detectable effect of mast cell depletion.
results.quote: mice froze at levels that were similar to those of WT mice, suggesting that mast cells likely contribute to fear-based memory deficits in 5XFAD mice

results.finding: A second mast cell depletion model reduced cortical GFAP in female 5XFAD mice (n in Fig. 4F, genotype interaction p = 0.0023).
results.detail: GFAP is a marker of astrocyte reactivity. The Kit experiment reproduced the marker and morphology changes. Independent laboratory reproduction of the behavioral effect remains unestablished in this source.
results.quote: we demonstrated that the absence of mast cells reduced expression of GFAP, a marker for reactive astrocytes, and altered astrocyte morphology in the brains of 5XFAD mice.

results.finding: Masitinib-treated SOD1 G93A rats had 40% lumbar motor neuron loss after paralysis onset. The motor neuron count sample size was unspecified.
results.detail: The paper gives four rats per condition for soma sizing. The stereological motor neuron count methods specify five sections but give no rat count.
results.quote: In comparison, masitinib significantly reduced motor neuron loss to 40 % when administered after paralysis onset.

results.finding: The nilotinib trial enrolled 37 participants and administered the drug under FDA IND #130732.
results.quote: The study was conducted under FDA Investigational New Drug (IND) #130732, and registered in  ClinicalTrials.gov  ( NCT02947893 ).

results.finding: The nilotinib arm (n=17) had 0 serious adverse events.
results.detail: Participants assigned to nilotinib received 150 mg daily for the first 26 weeks, then 300 mg daily for another 26 weeks. The authors suggested the lower dose for further study.
results.quote: No SAEs were observed in the nilotinib group and there were no dropouts due to intolerability.

results.finding: In the nilotinib trial (n=37 enrolled), cerebrospinal fluid Aβ40 fell by 566 ng/ml versus placebo at six months.
results.detail: The authors interpreted the amyloid changes as consistent with enhanced autophagic clearance. The study did not measure autophagic flux directly.
results.quote: In the nilotinib versus placebo groups, CSF Aβ40 was reduced at 6 months (566 ng/ml; 95% CI, 32 to 1,145;  p  = 0.03) compared to baseline (see Fig  3B ).

results.finding: In the nilotinib trial (n=37 enrolled), the exploratory ADAS-Cog maze comparison at six months yielded p = 0.03.
results.detail: The trial was designed around safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics and was underpowered for clinical efficacy.
results.quote: However, there was a significant difference in time to complete the maze between placebo and nilotinib‐treated groups (4.7 seconds; 95% CI, 0.42 to 12.85;  p  = 0.03) at 6 months.

results.finding: RT001 normalized mitochondrial membrane potential in 3 PSP-derived stem cell lines relative to 2 healthy controls (reduction after RT001, p = 0.0009).
results.detail: Mitochondrial membrane potential was measured by TMRM fluorescence. The p-value describes the treatment-associated reduction. Normalization to control levels is reported in the Results text.
results.quote: This increase remained elevated when the cells were incubated with H2-LA, but Δψm normalized after RT001 ( Figure 2 , Panels A and B).

results.finding: In PLP-hαSyn mice (n = 8–10/group), anle138b kept beam slips per step at healthy control levels, with a treatment comparison of P < 0.001.
results.detail: Treatment began before nigral degeneration, and motor performance was measured at the end of treatment. The result demonstrates prevention of the motor deficit.
results.quote:
PLP-hαSyn mice treated with both doses of anle138b
maintained normal motor function as compared to
healthy control mice (Fig. 1).

results.finding: JQ1 restored hippocampal long-term potentiation in APP/PS1–21 mice (5 slices from 3 mice per group, P < 0.05).
results.detail: The water maze and slice recordings measured related but distinct outcomes. Both experiments used JQ1, which inhibits multiple BET proteins.
results.quote:
LTP was enhanced in wild-type slices, reduced in APP-vehicle animals
and rescued in APP animals by bath application of JQ1.

results.finding: Src or c-Abl knockdown increased survival of patient-derived mutant SOD1 ALS motor neurons (n = 6 per group, p < 0.05).
results.detail: Expression of siRNA-resistant Src or c-Abl reversed the survival benefit of the corresponding knockdown.
results.quote:
Knock-down of Src or c-Abl increased the survival rate of mutant SOD1 ALS MNs (ALS1) 
(each group represents mean ± SEM, n = 6; one-way ANOV A, p<0.05, *p<0.05).

results.finding: In a Tau zebrafish model of PSP (n = 12 per group), (+)JQ1 rescued 75% of the light-phase swimming-speed deficit.
results.detail: The screening hit was validated with repurchased (+)JQ1. Brd4 disruption reproduced key effects in zebrafish. The rat culture experiment used (+)JQ1, which inhibits multiple BET proteins, so it did not independently establish a Brd4-specific effect.
results.quote:
The top hit, (+)JQ1, res-
cued light phase swimming speed by 75% at a bath concentration of
2 µM( F i g .7d, f).

results.finding: Collaborating physicians administered RT001 to 3 patients with progressive supranuclear palsy under expanded access.
results.detail: The 3 expanded-access patients received RT001 before Retrotope filed the Phase 2/3 IND. The release leaves the IND status of their expanded-access protocols unspecified.
results.quote: Retrotope filed this IND for a PSP Phase 2/3 trial after 3 patients treated by physicians collaborating with Retrotope in PSP Expanded Access protocols showed encouraging results after more than a year on drug.

results.finding: ATH434 Phase 2 trial in early-stage multiple system atrophy (planned n≈60) reported 1 U.S. participant dosed.
results.detail: The trial includes two ATH434 dose levels and placebo. The release gives no FDA receipt date, clinical-hold status, or notification allowing the investigation to begin.
results.quote:
“The U.S. is an important region for our ATH434 Phase 2 clinical trial, and we are thrilled to have 
dosed our first patient at Vanderbilt University Medical Center,”

results.finding: In mild Alzheimer disease (n=46), 0 of 34 participants receiving MAPTRx had a serious adverse event.
results.detail: The safety monitoring group authorized dose escalation within the trial, and a phase 2 trial was underway at publication. Neither fact establishes that the candidate met prespecified safety and tolerability criteria for advancement.
results.quote:
No serious adverse events were reported in MAPT
Rx
-treated patients.

results.finding: In phase 1 iDReAM (12 ALS patients evaluable for dose-limiting toxicity), the committee selected bosutinib 300 mg once daily for phase 2.
results.detail: The committee assessed dose-limiting toxicity at four weeks and over the full 12-week treatment period. At 400 mg, all three patients discontinued because of treatment-related adverse events.
results.quote: The general safety and tolerability of bosutinib in ALS was evaluated by 3 + 3 design, and the MTD and RP2D were determined to be 300 mg in this study.

results.finding: In the BIIB092 phase 1b trial for progressive supranuclear palsy (n=48), 100% of participants completed treatment.
results.detail: Safety was the primary outcome. The authors judged repeated dosing generally well tolerated, but the text gives no prespecified threshold for advancement.
results.quote: All 48 participants completed the treatment phase of the study.

results.finding: In early multiple system atrophy, intrathecal autologous mesenchymal stem cells (n=24) caused 0 attributable serious adverse events.
results.detail: The authors judged lower doses adequately tolerated and cited efficacy signals in support of a planned phase II/III trial.
results.quote: Twenty-four patients received treatment. There were no attributable serious adverse events, and injections were generally well-tolerated.

results.finding: In the ALS trial (196 randomized), cerebrospinal fluid MCP-1 with MSC-NTF was 74% of placebo.
results.detail: The MCP-1 comparison was measured at week 20. The biomarker P values were nominal after the trial missed its primary clinical endpoint.
results.quote: At all timepoints, CSF MCP‐1 was significantly reduced with MSC‐NTF relative to placebo ( P  < .05, overall treatment effect  P  < .0001), with week 20 MSC‐NTF values 74% of placebo (Figure  2B ).

results.finding: In progressive supranuclear palsy, mean free tau in cerebrospinal fluid fell 80.41% one week after the first bepranemab dose (n=15 evaluable).
results.detail: Target engagement was an exploratory endpoint. Three participants in each group lacked a calculable change from baseline, and the study reported descriptive statistics.
results.quote:
Reduction (80.41%) in 
mean free tau cerebrospinal fluid levels was observed in the 
bepranemab group.

results.finding: In familial multiple system atrophy (n=1), brain oxygen metabolism increased by approximately 30% after ubiquinol.
results.detail: The open-label study compared PET measurements with the same patient's pretreatment baseline and had no concurrent control.
results.quote:
the CMRO
2
markedly increased by approximately 30% in the entire brain

results.finding: Ubiquinol met the primary efficacy threshold in multiple system atrophy (n = 129 analyzed, P = 0.023).
results.detail: The Results and Table 2 identify 129 efficacy participants, while the abstract reports 131 and the Figure 2 caption gives a different effect estimate. The assessment uses the primary analysis in Results and Table 2.
results.quote: This study met the primary efficacy outcome (least square mean difference in UMSARS part 2 score (−1.7 [95% CI, −3.2 to −0.2]; P = 0.023)).

results.finding: In a 959-patient ALS trial, riluzole 100 mg/day improved tracheostomy-free survival by 6.4 percentage points versus placebo.
results.detail: The survival result was statistically significant after adjustment for prognostic factors. The unadjusted comparison had p = 0.076.
results.quote: At the end of the study, after median follow-up of 18 months, 122 (50.4%) placebo-treated patients and 134 (56.8%) of those who received 100 mg/day riluzole were alive without tracheostomy (unadjusted risk 0.79, p = 0.076; adjusted risk 0.65, p = 0.002).

definition = "Treatments acting on the same biological process slow clinical decline in at least two distinct diseases that progressively destroy nerve cells. Experiments show that changing the process affects a disease-relevant function, such as neuron survival. Studies in people with each diagnosis show both that treatment changes the process and that patients decline more slowly.". Reason: The definition uses target validation and human pathway modulation without explaining what either measurement establishes.

goal.need = "In 2021 an estimated 6.25 million Americans were living with Alzheimer dementia, which progressively erodes the ability to manage daily tasks. ALS takes away voluntary movement and has a median survival of 20\u201348 months. Riluzole prolonged survival in ALS trials without a measurable benefit in muscle strength. Where the same process injures neurons in different diseases, slowing that injury could give people more time to manage daily tasks or move independently. The benefit depends on how much the process contributes to decline in each disease.". Reason: The existing text reports testimony without explaining what patients lose, what current treatment preserves, or why a shared target matters to them.

add statement by National Institute on Aging, FY 2020 Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Bypass Budget Milestones, milestone 2.H, 2018: "Launch a minimum of three drug discovery projects targeting pathways common across AD and at least two other neurodegenerative disorders.". Reason: NIA milestone 2.H gives a specific cross-disease drug-discovery goal that the existing statements omit.
remove not found 2. Reason: The published FY 2020 budget chart supplies the text and success criteria of NIA’s common-mechanisms milestone 2.H.

add not found: "No regulator, professional society or research roadmap was found that judged shared-mechanism therapy across neurodegenerative diseases unachievable or unworthy of pursuit.". Reason: Negative trials of individual drugs leave a different question open about institutional opposition to the broader goal.
add case "Progressive supranuclear palsy". Reason: NNIPPS tested riluzole against placebo in a prespecified progressive supranuclear palsy stratum.
add case "Multiple system atrophy". Reason: NNIPPS separately assessed survival and functional decline in participants with multiple system atrophy.

edit m1: title = "Changing a candidate shared target corrects a disease-relevant function in an experimental model."; criterion = "In a cell or animal model of the diagnosis, changing the expression or activity of the candidate target normalizes a functional measurement selected to represent the disease state."; set_by = "NINDS, RFA-NS-19-015, phenotypic target-validation criterion for Alzheimer\u2019s disease-related dementias. Its use in other diagnoses is by analogy."; threshold_quote = "modulation leads to the normalization or impairment of the functional read outs selected to represent respectively the disease or control states"; threshold_ref = 4; refs = [4]. Reason: The mouse clasping result obscures the functional test, and a single model experiment can be judged separately from cross-laboratory validation.

add milestone after m1: "Independent laboratories reproduce the functional effect of changing the target using different methods.". Reason: The NINDS programme identifies replication across laboratories and methods as a distinct validation step after technical feasibility.

edit m2: criterion = "An investigator administers the candidate treatment to a participant under an effective US investigational new drug application (IND).
